rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections: just cause, relocation assistance, right to re-rent and buyout rules (SDMC ch. 9, art. 8, div. 7)
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not terminate a covered tenancy without just cause.

At-fault causes: nonpayment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to sign a substantially similar renewal (leases ending on or after June 24, 2023), criminal activity, criminal threats, unauthorized assignment or sublet, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, an employee's failure to vacate, and failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice. For a curable violation, the landlord must first give written notice and a chance to cure, and may then serve a three-day notice to quit.

No-fault causes, taken in good faith:
- Owner or relative move-in for at least 12 continuous months. For leases from June 24, 2023, the tenant must agree in writing or the lease must allow it. The occupant must move in within 90 days, otherwise the unit is re-offered at the same rent and terms.
- Withdrawal from the rental market.
- A government or court order or local ordinance requiring the unit to be vacated.
- Demolition or substantial remodel. Permits must be secured first, and the notice is certified under penalty of perjury with the specified contents.

No-fault notice: written, 30 or 60 days ahead per Civ. Code § 1946.1, in at least 12-point font. It must state the basis, the relocation right and the five-year right to an offer to re-rent.

Relocation assistance applies regardless of income or length of tenancy. It is 2 months of actual rent, or 3 months if the tenant is a senior (62+) or disabled. The landlord either pays it directly within 15 days of the notice or waives that amount of rent.

Right of first offer: if the unit is re-offered within 5 years of an eviction under § 98.0704(b)(1), (3) or (4), the displaced tenant gets the first offer if they asked in writing within 30 days. The tenant then has 30 days to accept.

Tenant notice: landlords must give every covered tenant the § 98.0705 rights notice and the Housing Commission's Tenant Protection Guide.

Commission notice: landlords must notify the Housing Commission of at-fault and no-fault terminations within 3 business days. This applies only from 30 days after the Commission announces a submission portal.

Buyouts: a written disclosure is required before any buyout offer. Buyout agreements must be in writing, contain the 14-point bold statements, be translated where required, and exceed the relocation amount, or they are void.

Retaliation is prohibited. Any noncompliance voids the termination notice.
rules.key_value: No-fault relocation: 2 months' actual rent (3 months for seniors 62+ or disabled tenants), paid directly within 15 days of notice or by rent waiver; 30/60-day notice (Civ. Code § 1946.1); 5-year right of first offer after (b)(1), (3) or (4) evictions (30 days to accept); wrongful eviction liability at least 3x actual economic damages; failure to pay relocation at least 3x the required assistance plus actual economic damages; buyouts must exceed the relocation amount

new_construction_exemption.basis: certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (rolling; not applicable to mobilehomes)

unverifiable_exemptions: Housing restricted by deed, regulatory agreement or other document as affordable housing for very low, low or moderate income households
Housing subject to an affordable-housing subsidy agreement (Section 8 voucher tenancies are not exempt)

Separately alienable property (including a mobilehome) whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management, where tenants received the § 98.0703(l) written exemption notice (in the lease for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after Jan. 1, 2024)
Nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or non-profit transitional housing
Dormitories owned and operated by a higher-education or K-12 institution
Tenant shares bathroom or kitchen with a landlord who lives there as principal residence
Owner-occupied single-family residence renting no more than two bedrooms, two ADUs or two JADUs (or a mobilehome); owner-occupied two-unit structure while the landlord remains in occupancy
coverage.summary: Applies citywide to tenancies in residential rental property, meaning a right to occupy for more than 30 days, excluding fixed terms of 3 months or less. Mobilehome park units are included. No minimum occupancy period is required, unlike the state's 12-month threshold. Exempt: housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (rolling, except mobilehomes) and the categories listed in § 98.0703. Covered property follows this local ordinance rather than Civ. Code § 1946.2.
coverage.owner_conditions: Exempt: single-family residence occupied by the landlord as principal residence (renting no more than two bedrooms, two ADUs or two JADUs); two-unit structure where the landlord occupied one unit at the start of the tenancy and still does; separately alienable property of a non-REIT, non-corporate landlord (not an LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management) that gave the required written notice.
coverage.other_conditions: Exempt: transient and tourist hotel occupancy, and short-term residential occupancy under SDMC ch. 5, art. 10, div. 1. Mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law are exempt, but mobilehomes are excluded from the 15-year new-construction exemption.

rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy; short-term residential occupancy; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (Section 8 not exempt); mobilehomes subject to the MRL; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, RCFE, adult residential facility and non-profit transitional housing; school-owned dormitories; shared bathroom or kitchen with a resident landlord; owner-occupied single-family residence or two-unit structure; housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); qualifying separately alienable property with written exemption notice.
rules.effective_date_note: Division retitled and substantially re-enacted by O-21647 N.S., adopted 5-25-2023 and effective 6-24-2023. Amended by O-21769 N.S. on 2-27-2024, effective 3-28-2024: definitions, § 98.0704 and remedies amended, and § 98.0710 added. The original Tenants' Right to Know Regulations date from 3-30-2004 (O-19269 N.S.). The Commission-notice duties in § 98.0706(a)(2) and (b)(2) start only 30 days after the Housing Commission publicly announces a submission portal. Per the Legal Aid fact sheet (Sept. 2023), the ordinance has no sunset.

rules.quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause.
rules.review_note: The documents do not show whether the Housing Commission has launched the termination-notice submission portal. The Legal Aid fact sheet estimated July 2024 and said the requirement was not yet in effect. Check before treating the 3-business-day Commission notice as operative. The 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption is a rolling window, so a building's coverage changes over time. The code text is the 3-2024 edition; amendments after O-21769 N.S. are not reflected.
rules.source_notes: Official SDMC Division 7 text (D073) is primary. A cell candidate gave relocation as 3 months' rent, citing a City summary of the earlier 2021 ordinance. The current official text (§ 98.0706(c)) sets 2 months, or 3 months for seniors and disabled tenants, and the Legal Aid fact sheet (DX17) agrees. The fact sheet also says the owner-occupied duplex exemption requires that neither unit be an ADU or JADU, but SDMC § 98.0703(j) contains no such condition; the official text governs. The fact sheet's reference to Civ. Code § 1947.12 is only the required notice text, and no local rent cap exists.

rules.title: San Diego Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing (SDMC ch. 9, art. 8, div. 11)
rules.requirement:
It is unlawful for any person to sell, license or otherwise provide an algorithmic device to a landlord. It is also unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.

An algorithmic device is software or a product that uses algorithms to calculate nonpublic competitor data of two or more landlords in order to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels for San Diego residential rental property.

Each month a landlord's use continues, and each property where a device is used, is a separate violation.

Tenants may sue a landlord for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. A prevailing landlord or tenant recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and lease clauses limiting fee recovery are unenforceable. Remedies are cumulative. The City may also enforce under SDMC ch. 1, art. 2, including civil and criminal remedies.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each residential rental property is a separate violation; prevailing landlord or tenant recovers costs and attorney's fees; City civil and criminal enforcement; effective June 21, 2025

coverage.summary: Applies citywide to anyone who sells, licenses or provides algorithmic devices to landlords, and to landlords of residential rental property in the City of San Diego. No unit-count, construction-date or owner-type limits are stated. The Division borrows only the § 98.0702 definitions, not the Division 7 exemptions. State Cartwright Act rules on common pricing algorithms (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729) operate alongside it.
coverage.other_conditions: Landlord, lease, residential rental property and tenant have the meanings in SDMC § 98.0702. Residential rental property includes units in mobilehome parks.

rules.exemptions: Not an algorithmic device: (a) software publishing reports from aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, or from public information, that does not recommend rates or occupancy for future leases or renewals; (b) software used to set rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines; (c) appraisal software that does not recommend rental rates during runtime.
rules.effective_date_note: Added 5-22-2025 by O-21955 N.S., effective 6-21-2025, per the Municipal Code history notes. This matches the ordinance's 30-days-after-final-passage clause in the draft (O-2025-107) and the law-firm alert's 'effective June 2025'.

rules.review_note: The ordinance is being litigated in Keller v. UDR Inc. (S.D. Cal.), per a law-firm alert of Aug. 2026. The documents report no ruling on its validity.
rules.source_notes: Adopted Municipal Code text (DX05, 6-2025 edition) is primary. The staff report and draft O-2025-107 (D076) are the proposed version of the same ordinance and are merged here. The adopted text differs from the draft in four ways: the definition is limited to nonpublic competitor data 'of two or more landlords'; an appraisal-software exclusion is added; attorney's fees go to a prevailing landlord or tenant (the draft said prevailing tenant only); and § 98.1104(c) adds City enforcement. The Morgan Lewis alert (DX06) is secondary and consistent.
